questions.prompt: Which word belongs in “Stir the ___ into the cake mixture”?
questions.explanation: Flour is the baking ingredient. The cake mixture gives you the clue.

questions.prompt: What makes flour and flower homophones?
options: They share a pronunciation but have different meanings
questions.explanation: Listen to the sound, then compare the meanings: a baking ingredient and something with petals.

questions.prompt: In “I would like a biscuit too”, what does too mean?
questions.explanation: Too can mean also. The sentence is about wanting a biscuit as well, rather than counting two.

title: What are homophones? Words that sound the same
practice: Try Connections and look for a relationship that fits every clue. It might involve meaning, a category or another shared feature.

sections.html:
Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings. Flour is a baking ingredient; a flower has petals. Same sound, very different shopping lists.

Turn up with flour when someone wanted a flower and you have the beginning of a cake, but a rather disappointing bouquet.

The flour and flower dictionary entries give the same pronunciation. Other pairs include knight/night and two/too.
sections.title: Same sound, different meaning

sections.html:
Use the meaning of the whole sentence. The surrounding words provide context: a vase suggests a flower, while a cake recipe suggests flour.

Same sound, different jobs
SentenceWord to chooseHelpful clue
Put the ___ in the vase.flowerA vase holds flowers.
Stir the ___ into the cake mixture.flourFlour is a baking ingredient.
I would like ___ biscuits.twoWe are counting biscuits.
I would like a biscuit ___.tooThis person would also like one.

The last two words appear in Merriam-Webster’s explanation of homophones, alongside to. Matching sounds do not guarantee matching spelling.
sections.title: How do you choose the right spelling?

sections.html:
Find one word for each clue. Each pair should sound the same. Say your answers aloud before opening the answers.

  1. A baking ingredient / something with petals.
  2. A horse-shaped chess piece / the dark part of the day.
  3. A number after one / another way to say “also”.
Check the three pairs

1. Flour / flower. One goes into your cake; the other can go in a vase.

2. Knight / night. The chess piece is a knight. Night is the time between dusk and dawn. The dictionary gives knight and night the same pronunciation.

3. Two / too. Two counts things. Too can mean also: “I want to come too.”

Now make up a silly sentence using both words from one pair. “The knight only rides at night” keeps the two meanings clear, even though they sound alike.
sections.title: Try three pairs with your ears

sections.html:
Look at flour, sugar, butter and eggs. They belong together because they can all be baking ingredients. Now look at flour and flower. This time the connection is sound.

In a word puzzle, try explaining the relationship in one short sentence. Then check that it fits every clue. Our Connections guide shows how to test a possible link.
sections.title: A word puzzle can connect sounds or meanings

sections.html:
Homophones share a sound; homographs share a spelling. The terms can overlap. Merriam-Webster’s guide to the different word pairs explains the distinction.

Accents matter, too. A pair that sounds identical to one speaker may sound different to another. Check a dictionary’s audio if a puzzle’s suggested pair does not work in your accent.

For a different word surprise, try words that can mean their own opposite. This time the twist is in the meaning.
sections.title: What about words that look alike?

description: Homophones sound alike but mean different things. Untangle flour and flower, knight and night, then use a sentence clue to choose the right word.
